newsitem.title: PERU: Peru says new talks would put crisis in last stage.
newsitem.headline: Peru says new talks would put crisis in last stage.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori said on Saturday he wanted to catapult the 95-day hostage crisis into its final stage by restarting peace talks with Marxist rebels holding 72 VIPs at the Japanese ambassador's home.

After a 10-day break from negotiations, the two sides still lacked enough common ground for fresh face-to-face talks, Fujimori said. But his negotiator Domingo Palermo suggested a resumption might not be too far off.
"We are ready and hoping that at any moment the talks can resume," said Palermo, who was accompanying Fujimori on a whirlwind tour of education centres in Lima's shanty-towns.

Fujimori told reporters: "To have direct talks we must find common ground and have the terrain prepared. If this were the case, we would enter in what we call the 'final issues'. This is what we want."

During the suspension of talks -- dubbed a period of "reflection" -- the two sides have worked separately with the talks' guarantors to explore possible concessions that would bring a peaceful end to the standoff.

Fujimori continues to reject the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) hostage-takers' main demand for the release of some 450 jailed comrades. But there are signs he is prepared to make other concessions.

For the first time since early in the crisis, the government allowed Red Cross officials on Friday to visit MRTA rebels in prison after the talks' guarantors formed a special committee to check on their health and conditions.
Improving prison conditions for the rebels is believed to be one of the main concessions Fujimori is willing to make to the MRTA.

The Peruvian and Japanese governments also concluded this week their work to assure the rebels asylum abroad if a peaceful solution is brokered. Japanese Vice Foreign Minister Masahiko Komura visited Cuba and the Dominican Republic and received formal offers of asylum from those Caribbean nations.

The moves away from the negotiating table have led to intense speculation in Lima that the government has finally hammered out a package of concessions that could persuade the rebels to give up their hostages.

The New York Times reported that mediators have outlined a tentative agreement to end the crisis whereby rebels would take asylum in Cuba in exchange for early parole for some comrades jailed on lesser charges.

But an MRTA leader in Peru's central jungle poured cold water on at least one part of the deal. Comrade Alejandro, a member of the MRTA's highest policy-making body, told Reuters on Friday that asylum was not up for discussion because the government had yet to consider the group's demand for freeing jailed comrades.

And in a sign the hostage-takers were still defiant on Saturday, they put a placard up to a window of the besieged residence lambasting the Peruvian army for alleged human rights abuses during a recent sweep in the jungle.
"Stop the torture and arbitrary detention of civilians in the central jungle," it read.

A leading Peruvian human rights group and villagers in the counties of Junin and Pasco about 200 miles (300 km) east of Lima support the MRTA's claim that the army has tortured peasants in an ongoing offensive to flush the rebels out of their strongholds.
Fujimori dismissed the accusations as an attempt to disparage the security forces and the army said it fully respected human rights in the capture of 38 "MRTA terrorists".
